249	    def search(self, cond: QueryLike) -> list[Document]:
250	        """
251	        Search for all documents matching a 'where' cond.
252	
253	        Note: a repeated search with the same ``cond`` is served from an
254	        internal cache. The returned list is a fresh copy, but its
255	        documents are the same objects held by the cache -- treat them as
256	        read-only, since mutating one (a key or a nested value) corrupts
257	        what a later identical search returns.
258	
259	        :param cond: the condition to check against
260	        :returns: list of matching documents
261	        """
262	
263	        # First, we check the query cache to see if it has results for this
264	        # query
265	        cached_results = self._query_cache.get(cond)
266	        if cached_results is not None:
267	            return cached_results[:]
268	
269	        # Perform the search by applying the query to all documents.
270	        # Then, only if the document matches the query, convert it
271	        # to the document class and document ID class.
272	        docs = [
273	            self.document_class(doc, self.document_id_class(doc_id))
274	            for doc_id, doc in self._read_table().items()
275	            if cond(doc)
276	        ]
277	
278	        # Only cache cacheable queries.
279	        #
280	        # This weird `getattr` dance is needed to make MyPy happy as
281	        # it doesn't know that a query might have a `is_cacheable` method
282	        # that is not declared in the `QueryLike` protocol due to it being
283	        # optional.
284	        # See: https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/1424
285	        #
286	        # Note also that by default we expect custom query objects to be
287	        # cacheable (which means they need to have a stable hash value).
288	        # This is to keep consistency with TinyDB's behavior before
289	        # `is_cacheable` was introduced which assumed that all queries
290	        # are cacheable.
291	        is_cacheable: Callable[[], bool] = getattr(cond, 'is_cacheable',
292	                                                   lambda: True)
293	        if is_cacheable():
294	            # Update the query cache
295	            self._query_cache[cond] = docs[:]
296	
297	        return docs

input.title: Optional `limit` argument for search()
input.summary: Precise feature request: `search(cond, limit=N)` returns at most N matching documents in the same order as today; omitting `limit` must leave behaviour unchanged. I read tinydb/table.py: `Table.search(self, cond)` has no `limit` today. It returns a fresh list copy of cached results, and caches cacheable queries. `TinyDB.search` is forwarded to the default table through `__getattr__` (database.py:251). That makes cache interaction an observable concern: a limited search must not change what a later unlimited search returns. The previous draft failed on FR-SRCH-003.AC-2 ('existing calls' had no baseline). Both FR-SRCH-003 criteria now use a fixed table (five documents, n=1..5) and literal expected values, so they have no hidden baseline. Edge-case inputs (limit=0, negative, non-int, None) and whether evaluation must stop early are P2/P3 questions that block no stated behaviour. Stakeholder mode is unavailable, so the verdict is READY-WITH-OPEN-ITEMS: all core requirements are READY and no P1 question or conflict is open.

requirements.statement: The system shall let Table.search accept an optional `limit` argument and, when a positive integer `limit` is given, return at most `limit` matching documents.

acceptance_criteria.given: a fresh in-memory table (TinyDB(storage=MemoryStorage).table('t')) holding five documents {'n':1}..{'n':5} inserted in that order, and cond = Query().n >= 1 (all five match)
the same fixture and cond, where table.search(cond) was already called once without limit (so the result is held in the query cache)
acceptance_criteria.then: the returned list has length 2 and equals [{'n':1},{'n':2}]

acceptance_criteria.given: the same fixture and a fresh cond = Query().n >= 1
acceptance_criteria.then: the returned list has length 1 and its element has doc_id 1 and content {'n':1}

requirements.statement: The system shall return the documents of a limited search in the same relative order in which search() without `limit` returns them.
requirements.source_quote: in the same order `search()` returns them today

acceptance_criteria.given: a fresh in-memory table holding documents {'n':1}..{'n':5} inserted in that order (doc_ids 1..5), and cond = Query().n >= 1
acceptance_criteria.then: the returned documents have doc_ids [1, 2, 3] and contents [{'n':1},{'n':2},{'n':3}], in that order

acceptance_criteria.given: the same fixture, and a second fresh table built identically for the baseline
acceptance_criteria.when: table.search(cond, limit=3) is called on the first and table.search(cond)[:3] on the second
acceptance_criteria.then: the two lists are equal element by element, including doc_id

requirements.statement: The system shall return, for a call to search without a `limit` argument, the same result it returned before the `limit` argument was introduced.
requirements.source_quote: Without `limit` it should behave exactly as it does now.

acceptance_criteria.given: a fresh in-memory table holding documents {'n':1}..{'n':5} inserted in that order (doc_ids 1..5)
acceptance_criteria.when: table.search(Query().n >= 3) is called with no `limit` argument
acceptance_criteria.then: the result is a list of exactly three Document objects with doc_ids [3, 4, 5] and contents [{'n':3},{'n':4},{'n':5}], in that order

acceptance_criteria.given: the same fixture and one Query object cond = Query().n >= 1
acceptance_criteria.when: table.search(cond) is called twice with no `limit` argument, giving results r1 and r2
acceptance_criteria.then: r1 and r2 each have doc_ids [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and contents [{'n':1}..{'n':5}], and r1 is not r2 (the second call returns a new list object)

requirements.statement: The system shall return the complete list of matching documents from a search without `limit` that is made after a search with `limit` using the same condition.
requirements.source_quote: Without `limit` it should behave exactly as it does now. (parent: FR-SRCH-003; a limited result left in the query cache would make a later unlimited search differ from today's behaviour)

acceptance_criteria.given: a fresh in-memory table holding documents {'n':1}..{'n':5} inserted in that order, and one Query object cond = Query().n >= 1 on which no search has yet been made
acceptance_criteria.when: table.search(cond, limit=2) is called and then table.search(cond) is called
acceptance_criteria.then: the second call returns five documents with doc_ids [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

requirements.statement: The system shall return all matching documents when the positive integer `limit` is greater than or equal to the number of matches.
requirements.source_quote: returning at most 10 matching documents (parent: FR-SRCH-001; 'at most' means fewer matches are returned as they are, not padded or refused)

acceptance_criteria.given: a fresh in-memory table holding documents {'n':1}..{'n':5} inserted in that order, and cond = Query().n <= 3 (three match)
acceptance_criteria.then: the result has doc_ids [1, 2, 3] and contents [{'n':1},{'n':2},{'n':3}]

acceptance_criteria.given: the same fixture and cond = Query().n <= 3

requirements.statement: The system shall accept the `limit` argument on search() called on a TinyDB instance, which operates on its default table.

acceptance_criteria.given: db = TinyDB(storage=MemoryStorage) with five documents {'level':'error','n':1}..{'level':'error','n':5} inserted in that order into the default table
acceptance_criteria.then: the result is a list of two documents with contents [{'level':'error','n':1},{'level':'error','n':2}], in that order
the result contains all five documents in insertion order

requirements.statement: The system shall define the behaviour of search() when `limit` is 0, negative, None, or not an integer.

acceptance_criteria.given: a fresh in-memory table holding documents {'n':1}..{'n':5} and cond = Query().n >= 1

requirements.statement: The system shall stop evaluating the query against further documents once `limit` matches have been found.

acceptance_criteria.given: a fresh in-memory table holding documents {'n':1}..{'n':5} and a counting condition object that records each document it is called on

interpretations: A positive integer maximum count; 0, negative, None and non-integer values are errors
limit=0 returns [] and limit=None means no limit; negatives are errors
Python slice semantics (negative counts from the end)

terms.term: same order search() returns them today
interpretations: The order of documents in the table's stored mapping (insertion order, doc_id ascending in the normal case) as returned by search() without limit
Ascending doc_id order regardless of storage order

terms.term: behave exactly as it does now
interpretations: Same return value (type, documents, doc_ids, order, fresh list copy) for the same inputs; this is what the acceptance criteria test
Additionally the same internal side effects (cache content, number of condition calls)
The first N matches in the order search() returns them (what FR-SRCH-002 covers)
Any N matches, with no guarantee of position

open_questions.question: What should search() do when `limit` is 0, negative, or not an integer (e.g. 1.5, '10', True)?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The issue only describes positive limits. Without an answer, FR-SRCH-007 cannot be tested. It does not block FR-SRCH-001 to FR-SRCH-006, whose acceptance criteria use positive limits only.
options: (a) limit=0 returns []; negative or non-int raises ValueError/TypeError
(c) negative values follow Python slice semantics

open_questions.question: Should an explicit `limit=None` be accepted and mean 'no limit'?
open_questions.why_it_matters: A None default is a common way to implement an optional argument, and callers may pass None through. It is an edge case that does not affect the stated behaviour.
options: (a) yes, same as omitting the argument

open_questions.question: The issue complains that `db.search(q)[:10]` 'builds the full list every time'. Must a limited search also avoid evaluating the query on documents after the limit-th match, or is returning the right result enough?
open_questions.why_it_matters: This decides whether early termination is a requirement and so whether it needs an acceptance criterion (e.g. the number of times cond is called). The stated behaviour (FR-SRCH-001..006) does not depend on it.
options: (a) early termination required: cond is called on no more documents than needed to find `limit` matches on an uncached query
(b) only the returned result is specified; performance is a goal, not a requirement
open_questions.proposed_default: (b), recorded as ASM-003 (PROVISIONAL), with FR-SRCH-008 kept as an unagreed candidate

open_questions.question: Who decides on this feature (the requester iDheer, or another maintainer)?
open_questions.why_it_matters: With a single requester the requester decides; recorded for completeness because no maintainer comments are available.

assumptions.text: For limit values outside the positive-integer range (0, negative, None, non-int), the provisional behaviour is: 0 returns [], None means no limit, negative or non-int values raise an error.
assumptions.risk_if_wrong: Callers relying on a different convention (e.g. slice semantics or an error for 0) would be surprised; only FR-SRCH-007 is affected.

assumptions.text: 'Behave exactly as it does now' is read as the observable return value (list type, Document objects, doc_ids, order, fresh copy per call), not internal side effects (TERM-3).
assumptions.risk_if_wrong: If internal side effects such as cache contents or condition-call counts are meant to be identical, FR-SRCH-003 would need more acceptance criteria.

assumptions.text: Early termination of query evaluation is not required; the issue's performance remark is a motivation (GOAL-1) and not a testable requirement.
assumptions.risk_if_wrong: If early termination is required, FR-SRCH-008 becomes core and a simple slice of the full result would not satisfy the issue.

assumptions.text: The issue author is the decision owner for this feature and no other stakeholders exist.
assumptions.risk_if_wrong: A maintainer may reject or change the API (e.g. a different argument name), invalidating the acceptance criteria that call `limit=`.

out_of_scope: Adding `limit` to other methods (Table.all, Table.get, Table.count, Table.update, Table.remove, etc.): the issue only names search().
Offset or pagination arguments, and sorting or reordering of results.
Changing the result order of search() without `limit`.
Changing the query cache design beyond what FR-SRCH-004 requires of its observable behaviour; this stage does not design the fix.
Performance targets or benchmarks for a 50k-document table: no numbers were given (see Q-003).
Changes to storage backends or the CLI the author mentions.
